agents.stance: PRAGMATIST: practical, resource-aware, shippable. Favor ideas that a small team could start on Monday. Prefer clarity and feasibility over cleverness.
CONTRARIAN: challenge the obvious. Invert the default assumption, argue the opposite of the expected move, and surface what everyone is ignoring.
DOMAIN-EXPERT: a deep specialist. Apply hard-won craft knowledge and non-obvious best practice; cite the mechanism, not just the vibe.
OUTSIDER-ANALOGY: import a mechanism from an unrelated field (biology, logistics, games, nature) and reason by analogy into this problem.
VISIONARY: aim for 10x, not 10%. Describe the ambitious end-state and work backward to a bold first move.

candidates.text: Run a weekly 30-minute user interview sprint where team members each talk to 2-3 users in rotation. Track patterns across interviews in a shared doc. Ship whatever feature request appears in 3+ independent interviews that month.

Deploy a lightweight in-app survey (3 questions max) asking users to rank their top 3 problems with the product. Analyze responses weekly and build the feature that solves the #1 ranked problem from the last 50 responses.

Pick the 5 most engaged users (by usage metrics) and give them direct Slack access to your team's build channel. Ask them to react with emoji to feature ideas posted daily; build whatever gets the most consistent enthusiasm.
Set a 2-week constraint: each team member proposes one small feature they'd use personally, you code all 5 in parallel, then measure which one users adopt fastest. Double down on the winner.
Create a public roadmap with 3 concrete half-finished ideas and ask users to vote daily via a simple link. After 10 days, whichever idea has the most votes gets completed and shipped.

Monitor your support inbox, Twitter mentions, and any community channels for feature requests. Tally them in a spreadsheet by category each week. Build the category with the most requests in the last month.

Build nothing and instead run a 'reverse roadmap' where users submit what they DON'T want removed or changed, then deliberately avoid building those things. This inverts the usual feature-request bias and reveals what's already working.

Make deciding what to build a paid service: charge users a small fee to vote on next features, ensuring only those with genuine skin-in-the-game weigh in, and filtering out noise from casual or disengaged users.

Randomly assign different user cohorts to use competing products for 30 days, then measure which features they actually migrate back asking for, rather than relying on stated preferences that rarely predict behavior.
Deliberately build the opposite of what users say they want for a small beta group, then measure whether satisfaction increases—many users don't know what will delight them until surprised.
Ignore users entirely and instead analyze what your power users are hacking around with third-party tools and integrations; build what they're already trying to bolt on, not what they claim to need.
Split the team: half builds based on zero data (intuition only), half builds based on all available data, then race both for 8 weeks and measure which approach generates more genuine user engagement.

Run a **jobs-to-be-done interview sprint**: Conduct 10–15 structured interviews asking users to describe a recent time they tried to solve a problem your product touches, what they actually used instead, and why that failed them. This surfaces latent needs better than direct feature requests because users reveal the real job context, not aspirational preferences.

Instrument **behavioral exhaust data** across your existing product: Identify the smallest cohort of power users, map their action sequences (e.g., tool combinations, time-to-aha, retry patterns), and build your next feature to unlock the bottleneck they hit most. Users reveal intent through friction, not surveys.

Deploy a **constraint-reversal roadmap workshop**: Have product and engineering list your three hardest technical or business constraints (e.g., 'we can't store video'), then brainstorm what becomes possible if each constraint disappears. This uncovers high-impact builds orthogonal to what users explicitly ask for.

Run a **sequential decision tree via rapid micro-commitments**: Launch three tiny, throwaway prototypes (each taking <1 week) that represent competing bets, measure which one users actually return to and spend time in, then double down on the winner's direction. This is faster and truer than asking what users want.

Conduct a **comparative teardown of competitor usage**: Find 5–10 users who use *both* your product and a direct competitor, and ask them to walk you through their typical week—when do they reach for each tool, and what task does the competitor solve that yours doesn't? This reveals job gaps your product leaves unfilled.

Build a **leading indicator tracker for churn risk**: Use cohort analysis to identify the feature or workflow *absence* most correlated with user drop-off (e.g., users who never export data churn 3x faster). Prioritize building that feature because it's solving a documented escape route, not a nice-to-have.

Use a 'predator-prey' dynamic where you release minimal features to different user cohorts and observe which ones get adopted/copied by other users (prey behavior) versus which ones trigger competitive alternatives (predator response). Track the ecosystem momentum to identify features with genuine staying power.

Implement a 'load-balancing algorithm' approach: distribute your engineering capacity across 4-6 small parallel experiments simultaneously, each with a different feature hypothesis, and let real usage metrics (response time, error rates, throughput) naturally kill the weakest performers while you double down on winners.

Adopt a 'mycorrhizal network' model where you don't decide alone—instead create lightweight feedback loops with power users, analysts, and adjacent teams who act as distributed sensors, sharing signals about unmet needs through structured monthly conversations that gradually reveal the most critical fungal threads to follow.

Use 'supply chain optionality' thinking: instead of committing to one roadmap, maintain a backlog structured like a supplier portfolio with redundancy and switching costs built in—prioritize whichever items have the shortest lead time and lowest switching cost, allowing you to pivot quickly as market signals arrive.

Borrow from 'evolutionary game theory': frame each potential feature as a strategy in a repeated game with your users, then run simulations or staged rollouts that show which strategies achieve stable equilibrium (long-term engagement) versus which collapse or trigger defection.

Apply a 'port-authority resource-allocation' model: treat your decision-making like a busy harbor deciding which ships to dock—prioritize based on frequency (how often users request it), cargo value (revenue/retention impact), and berthing speed (how fast you can build it), not by gut feeling.

Build a 'decision oracle' platform where the team submits their top 3 build candidates, and the system runs rapid micro-experiments (48-hour MVPs, A/B tests, user surveys, prototype feedback loops) in parallel across real user segments to generate comparative data instead of debating in a vacuum.

Establish a 'reverse advisory board' of 20-30 power users who get early access to rough prototypes and vote weekly on directional choices; treat them as continuous co-designers rather than one-time research subjects, fundamentally inverting who drives the roadmap.

Launch an internal 'build-off' where sub-teams each prototype a different candidate solution for the same user problem in 2 weeks, then deploy all versions to a subset of users simultaneously and let usage patterns—not opinions—determine which direction scales.

Create a real-time 'user signal aggregator' that pipes together passive behavioral data (app logs, support tickets, feature requests), sentiment from social listening, and structured weekly pulse surveys into a live dashboard that surfaces emergent patterns the team wouldn't see in isolation.

Implement 'problem-first hiring' where the team brings in 2-3 outside experts (domain specialists, adjacent-industry builders, contrarian thinkers) for a 2-week sprint specifically to interrogate assumptions and stress-test each candidate build direction before commitment.

Commit to a rotating 'build-in-public' model where each candidate feature ships to a tiny 1% cohort as a beta within days, then the team publicly documents what users actually do with it (not what they say), iterating based on real friction rather than hypothetical appeal.

Run a 'build debt audit' where you map every feature shipped in the last year against actual adoption curves—then identify the 2-3 features with the steepest drop-off and interview users who abandoned them. These failures reveal what *looked* valuable but wasn't; build the inverse: solve the real problem those failed features were supposed to solve.

Create a lightweight 'cannibalization tracker': when users request a new feature, immediately ask 'which existing workflow would this replace?' Ship only features that users explicitly say would let them delete or stop using something else. This filters for genuine simplification, not feature bloat.

Deploy a '48-hour lived experience' where 3-5 team members each shadow a different user for a full working day (async-friendly: screen recordings + time-stamped notes), focusing on *when they get stuck or switch tools mid-workflow*. Build the bridge that stops the context switch.

Implement a 'cost-per-ask' model: track how many support requests, survey mentions, and Slack pings each potential feature generates, then divide by engineering effort to get a 'signal density' score. Prioritize ruthlessly by efficiency: features with high ask volume + low build cost ship first, revealing quick wins that compound momentum.

Run a 'time-travel roadmap' where you ask your 10 most loyal users: 'If we disappeared for 6 months and came back with one thing, what would bring you back immediately?' This surfaces retention risk and high-leverage features, because it forces users to imagine loss, not aspiration.

Build a 'feature pairing algorithm' where you never decide on one feature in isolation—instead identify which small features are most likely to *unlock* or *multiply* the value of features already in the backlog, then ship them together as a compound bet. This finds high-leverage sequencing that users won't articulate but will feel.

Run a 'negative option' experiment: ship a feature nobody asked for to 10% of users without announcing it, then measure how many actively disable it versus silently adopt it. Build the inverse—features users explicitly requested but would actually toggle off if given the choice reveal what they *think* they want versus what they'll tolerate.

Create a 'temporal cohort map' where you segment users not by engagement level but by how long they've been with you, then deliberately interview the 5 users who churned in months 3-6 (the critical dropout window) about what they *almost* used before leaving. The near-miss tells you more than the vocal power user.

Instrument a 'frustration-delay correlation' tracker: log every moment a user pauses, hesitates, or repeats an action within your product, correlate those micro-pauses with feature requests submitted that week, and build the feature that eliminates the most frequent friction pattern—not the loudest complaint.

Establish a 'decoy roadmap' where you publicly announce building Feature X (something plausible but not in your actual queue), track which competitor or alternative tool users migrate to in response, and build the feature that competitor is *missing*—revealing gaps through market flight, not surveys.

Run monthly 'build sabotage sessions' where the team deliberately breaks one high-use feature for a 4-hour window on a Thursday afternoon, then documents which users complain, how fast they find workarounds, and what they're willing to lose—showing you what's actually load-bearing versus ornamental.

Create a 'cost-of-delay leaderboard' where you quantify the business/retention impact of *not* shipping each candidate feature (based on churn risk, support tickets, competitor wins), then rank by cost-of-delay per week rather than user volume—surfacing which feature's absence is quietly killing you while smaller requests get noise.

Run a 'negative option stack' experiment: ship a feature by default to all users, then measure how many actively disable it within 2 weeks. Features that survive high opt-out rates (>70% retention) are keepers; those that get killed reveal what users genuinely don't want. This inverts survey bias by measuring revealed preference through friction cost, not stated intent.

Instrument a 'dependency graph' of user workflows by tracking which features are used in sequence, then identify the missing link—the transition point where users drop off or switch tools. Prioritize building bridges at those exact handoff points, not at feature requests, because you're solving the actual job context where value breaks down.

Create a 'temporal cohort replay' where you segment users by signup date and analyze what feature adoption looked like for cohorts 12 months ago versus now. Features that early cohorts built around but later cohorts skip entirely signal product drift; rebuilding those bridges often unlocks dormant value without new features.

Deploy a 'willingness-to-wait' pricing experiment: gate 3-4 candidate features behind a 1-week delay, and let users pay a small amount to unlock them immediately. Payment velocity and timing reveal true demand far better than surveys, while those who don't pay get the feature anyway—giving you both signal and authentic user feedback.

Build a 'feedback momentum tracker' that doesn't just count feature requests, but measures velocity of repeated requests from the same user over time. A feature requested once by 10 users signals noise; a feature requested 5 times by 1 power user over 2 months signals compounding need. Prioritize based on request acceleration, not just volume.

Conduct a 'tool-switching audit' by identifying users who maintain concurrent subscriptions to your product and competitors, then instrument telemetry to log exactly which tasks they perform in each tool on the same day. Map the task-to-tool assignment, then build the task that's bleeding to competitors most, not what users say they want added.

Borrow from **predator-prey dynamics in ecosystems**: Release each candidate feature to a different user cohort as a 'prey species' and track which ones get adopted/remixed by adjacent teams or copied into workflows (prey thriving) versus which trigger users to hunt for competitor alternatives (predator response). Build the feature whose adoption pattern shows mutualistic spread, not escape behavior.

Apply **immunological memory**: Track which features users *return to repeatedly* after initial adoption (T-cell behavior) versus which they touch once and ignore (failed immune response). Prioritize building features that strengthen the immune memory of your product—i.e., features that become habitual anchors that make users *more* resistant to switching.

Adopt **supply-chain resilience thinking**: Map the critical path in your users' workflows (where do they get stuck waiting, or where do they manually bridge gaps between your tool and others?). Build the feature that removes the longest bottleneck in that critical path, treating feature prioritization like optimizing for throughput under constraint, not volume of requests.

Implement a **'decision diffusion' model from epidemiology**: Identify the 3-5 'patient zero' power users whose adoption patterns historically spread fastest through your user base. Run experiments *only* with them first, and measure the R-value (reproduction rate of adoption across their network) before committing engineering resources. Only build if the idea shows high contagion potential.

Use **particle-physics collision detection**: Have two sub-teams each build a competing feature in isolation for 3 weeks (no cross-talk). Then deploy *both simultaneously* to overlapping user cohorts and measure not which wins outright, but where users *combine* signals from both (using both features together in unexpected ways). Build the intersection, not the victor.

Borrow from **mycology's nutrient-cycling networks**: Instead of asking users what they want, map the invisible 'nutrient flows' in your ecosystem—what data, workflows, or outputs are users exporting to external tools and never bringing back? Build the feature that closes the loop and retains that nutrient (data/effort/intent) inside your product, treating recycling efficiency as the north star.

Run a 'temporal cohort autopsy' where you resurrect data from users who churned 6-12 months ago and map exactly which features they *stopped using first* before leaving—the inverse tells you which core workflows are load-bearing and which are decorative. Build to eliminate the #1 churn precursor, not to chase shiny requests.

Create a 'feature debt ledger' where every build candidate is scored not just on user demand but on how much technical or UX debt it creates or eliminates; then run a monthly auction where the team bids internal 'friction tokens' (representing time cost) on competing ideas, forcing honest prioritization of what actually compounds versus what merely feels urgent.

Instrument a 'silent witness protocol' where you embed a researcher in 5–10 users' actual working days (async, non-intrusive screen recordings or daily diaries) to capture the moment they abandon your product mid-workflow and reach for a workaround—map those escape hatches, then build the feature that plugs the most-traveled one.

Deploy a 'feature mutation sandbox' where you take one existing popular feature and release 4 radical variations (speed it up 10x, remove 80% of options, add AI, restrict to power users only) to different cohorts for 2 weeks, measuring not satisfaction but whether the mutation *increases the frequency* users return to that workflow—evolution over opinion.

Establish a 'cross-product DNA library' where you systematically catalog which features from 20+ adjacent tools your users explicitly import or emulate (via plugins, exports, manual workarounds), then identify the pattern—the unmet job—that ties them together, and build the native capability that makes the entire workaround chain obsolete.

Run a 'constraint-flip experiment' where you deliberately ship a feature with severe artificial limits (quota, time-gating, or permission walls) to small cohorts and measure whether users *fight harder to work within the constraint* (indicating genuine need) or abandon it immediately (indicating false demand)—only then remove the limit.
